title: Sis Ganj and Rakab Ganj
hook: where Guru Tegh Bahadur was killed and where his body was cremated

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bangla Sahib, the bungalow where the child Guru went out to the sick, and the pool beside it. Your line was the child's gurdwara. Who did you check on? Day one thousand three hundred twenty-eight.

Car horns. A man pushing a cart stacked with sacks. A wedding-card shop, a sweet shop, a stall selling phone covers, a rickshaw wedged sideways in the lane. Old Delhi's great market street, Chandni Chowk, is loud from morning to night. And right in the middle of it, between the shops, a gurdwara with a white front and a gold dome, its doors open, its singing drifting out into the traffic. Across the city stands a second gurdwara tied to the same day. Two buildings, one death. Today, why it takes two.
screen: `CAR HORNS, CARTS, A SWEET SHOP.` → `A GURDWARA AMONG THE STALLS.` → `TWO BUILDINGS, ONE DEATH.`

segments.voice: First, Sis Ganj. Sis is the Punjabi word for head. Year one told the story: Guru Tegh Bahadur, the ninth Guru, would not give up his faith, and would not let others be forced from theirs, and he was beheaded in the open square of Chandni Chowk. Gurdwara Sis Ganj stands at that spot, right in the market. Tradition says it keeps the trunk of the tree under which he was killed. That's today's line: where he gave his head. Second, Rakab Ganj. This path met both carriers on earlier days: Bhai Jaita, who took the head north to Anandpur, and Lakhi Shah Vanjara, who took the body home and set his own house alight. Tradition says Gurdwara Rakab Ganj stands where that house burned. Third, why it takes two. Danger split the Guru's body two ways, and the panth would not lose either. It marked the place of the death and the place of the fire, and kept walking to both. One stands in the loud middle of a market, open to anyone with a few minutes between errands. The other marks a fire lit in secret by a man with a cart. Fourth, a line from the Guru himself, from his saloks near the end of the Granth, here in paraphrase: whatever has come into being will pass away, today or tomorrow; so sing the praises of the Lord, and let the other tangles go. He wrote about the body passing. Then his own body passed, and two ordinary men made sure it was honored. Sis Ganj in the noise of the market. Rakab Ganj where a house went up in flames. Two addresses for one gift.
screen: `SIS GANJ: WHERE HE GAVE HIS HEAD.` · `RAKAB GANJ: WHERE THE HOUSE BURNED.` · `TWO PLACES, NEITHER LOST.` · `WHATEVER COMES INTO BEING PASSES.` · then, large: `TWO ADDRESSES FOR ONE GIFT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: picture Chandni Chowk. Settle, and breathe. Hear the horns, the carts, the shopkeepers calling. Let the noise be there. Now walk, in your mind, through the open doors of Sis Ganj, and let the noise fall behind you. Hear the singing. Stand quietly where the market once watched a man refuse to be moved. Then step back out into the street, and carry a little of that quiet with you. If you pray, you can rest on Waheguru. The bell holds the time.
Sis Ganj and Rakab Ganj. Two gurdwaras in Delhi: one where Guru Tegh Bahadur was beheaded, one where his body was secretly cremated. Today's word.
screen: `SIS GANJ AND RAKAB GANJ — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: where he gave his head. Today, in the noisiest place you go, take three slow breaths and remember one person who stood firm for someone else's freedom. Day one thousand three hundred twenty-eight.

howItsDone: Sikhs visiting Delhi go to Gurdwara Sis Ganj in Chandni Chowk and Gurdwara Rakab Ganj, and both are crowded on the day Guru Tegh Bahadur's martyrdom is remembered.

what it means: two gurdwaras for one death: Sis Ganj where the Guru gave his head, Rakab Ganj where his body was cremated.

notes: Days 79, 80, 155, 871 and 976 told the martyrdom, the carrying of the head, the marking of the sites and the Rakab Ganj wall. Today's angle: one death, two places, and who did the carrying.
'This path met both carriers on earlier days' refers to days 1319 (Lakhi Shah) and 1321 (Bhai Jaita); checked by the editor.
'Tradition says it keeps the trunk of the tree under which he was killed': please confirm Sis Ganj preserves the tree trunk.

Ang 1429, salok 52 ('jo upjio so binas hai parou aaj kai kaal; naanak har gun gaae le chhaad sagal janjaal') paraphrased; please confirm salok number and Ang. Salok 16 (frighten no one, fear no one) was avoided because it is used often on this path.
'Sis is the Punjabi word for head' is a word meaning, not an etymology; the meaning of 'Rakab' is deliberately not given.
Original ਸੀਸ ਗੰਜ: please confirm spelling.

Editor pass: days 1319 and 1321 had just told Lakhi Shah's burning house and Bhai Jaita's carrying in full, and 1321 made the 'who did the carrying' point, so the teach now refers back briefly and turns to why the panth keeps two places; the fork (Lakhi Shah's choice) was replaced with a Sis Ganj or Rakab Ganj question.
